opening.headline: How much should be allowed for coding agents to be safe is divided into permission rules, permission modes, and sandboxes.
body: Coding agents edit files, run shell commands, and access the network. Approving every request individually slows things down, and allowing them all is risky. The question of this class is where to draw the line between convenience and supervision, and what enforces that line.

In this lesson, we'll look at the order in which allow, confirm, and deny rules are evaluated, how permission modes change the criteria asked, and how they limit what a sandbox can reach once it's running. Next, we compare the extent of damage with and without a sandbox, and outline the criteria for selecting modes and isolation for each type of task.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain permission rules, permission modes, and sandbox isolation
You can analyze the priorities of allow, confirm, and deny rules.

screens.title: How much should we allow coding agents to be safe?
screens.lead: When you select each item, an explanation will unfold. Let's take a look at how the capabilities and risks of coding agents fit together.

visual.alt: A picture of the means of authority placed on a stick with convenience and supervision at both ends.
labels: Where do you draw the line?

items.prompt: What can a coding agent do?
items.answer: Read and edit files, run shell commands, and access the network. These three skills are essential for development, but if used incorrectly, they can lead to damage such as file deletion, credential leakage, and external service calls.

items.prompt: What happens if you approve every request individually?
items.answer: Manual mode prompts for most file modifications, shell commands, and network access before executing them. It is the safest, but operations often stutter and are slow. If there are too many questions, you may end up clicking without reading the content.

items.prompt: Conversely, what would happen if we allowed everyone?
items.answer: The operation is fast, but there is nothing to prevent the agent from executing invalid commands or unfamiliar code being executed through the agent. The damage extends to everything the user's account can reach.

items.prompt: What questions does this class ask?
items.answer: Where to draw the line between convenience and oversight, and what enforces that line. There are three means of drawing a line: There are permission rules that determine whether individual calls are allowed, a permission mode that sets the criteria for asking, and a sandbox that limits the reach after execution.

screens.outro: First, let me think about whether I have had a similar experience.

screens.title: Recall: Permission Request Fatigue
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Have you ever been asked for permission so frequently that you clicked on it without reading the content?
items.answer: It's a common experience. If requests are made frequently, people will approve the content without reading it, making confirmation meaningless. So, repeat safe requests should be automated with rules or modes, and questions should only pop up where confirmation is really needed.

items.prompt: Think of a scene where an agent almost touches a file in an unintended path.
items.answer: Examples include files outside the working directory or paths containing credentials. It is safe to block these paths with rules or limit the writing and reading range with a sandbox.

items.prompt: Think about what folders and sites you want to open.
items.answer: It is safer to first narrow down the folders and domains needed for work and expand them when necessary. It's difficult to open wide from the beginning and narrow down later. This is because permissions once opened are easy to forget.

screens.outro: Now that we've summarized our experience, let's start by looking at the permission rules that determine each call.

screens.title: Permission rules: allow, confirm, deny
screens.lead: Read the settings below to see how the rules are used and in what order they are evaluated. The explanation on the right also lists symptoms of incorrectly written rules.

visual.alt: Flow diagram in which rules are evaluated in the following order: deny, ask, and allow.
labels: If it matches, ask for confirmation
No match: default behavior in privileged mode
First, the matching result is determined

notes.note: The Allow rule allows tools to be used without permission. It is suitable for frequently used safe commands. If you use a pattern that is too broad, even unintended commands will be executed without asking.
The Ask rule checks every time. Even if there is a more specific allow rule, the ask rule requires confirmation first. It is suitable for commands that have external effects, such as push.

The Deny rule prevents its use. Rules are evaluated in the following order: deny, ask, and allow, and the matching result is determined first. Specificity does not take precedence, so denying Bash(aws *) also prevents allowing the narrower Bash(aws s3 ls).
deny using just the tool name (e.g. Bash) removes that tool from Claude's context entirely. With /permissions, you can check the current rules and the settings file where each rule is defined.

screens.outro: Now that we know the order in which rules are evaluated, let's compare permission modes that specify default behavior rather than rules.

screens.title: Behavior by permission mode
screens.lead: Select each tab to see how permission modes change the criteria they ask.

tabs.label: default (Manual)
tabs.body: It doesn't just ask for reads, most of the rest is asked before execution. Use it for sensitive tasks or when you want to directly review all actions. This is a conservative mode to choose when manually reviewing unfamiliar code. The startup mode of the latest interactive terminal/VS Code is auto, but headless/SDK/management settings may vary.

tabs.label: acceptEdits
tabs.body: It does not ask for file editing or common file system commands such as mkdir, mv, and cp. It is suitable for development where code is repeatedly modified locally. Shell commands or network access are still prompted according to the rules.

tabs.label: plan
tabs.body: Browsing is read-only, and editing is blocked until you approve the plan. Use this when you want to see what the agent is trying to do before changing the code.

tabs.label: auto
tabs.body: Classifier models examine behavior instead of humans. Reduces verification fatigue during long tasks. Since people do not see it in person, you must understand and write whether the review criteria are correct.

tabs.label: dontAsk
tabs.body: We only accept tools we pre-approve and reject the rest without questions. This is correct for CI without people. Be sure to write down your whitelist accurately so that no work is rejected.

tabs.label: bypassPermissions
tabs.body: This mode allows everything. It should only be used in isolated containers or VMs. Deny rules also apply in this mode. The write protected path and ask rule tools are not automatically approved in most modes.

screens.outro: The mode only sets the criteria to ask, it does not limit the reach. Let’s look at a sandbox that does just that.

screens.title: Sandbox: Isolate files and networks
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare the reach of shell commands without the sandbox and with it on.

visual.alt: Schematic showing where shell commands and other tools are executed, both inside and outside the sandbox boundaries.
labels: Allow writing: working directory, temporary directory
Proxy: Only accepted domains pass through
Running outside: controlled by permission rules

states.label: No sandbox
states.body: Shell commands can read and write anywhere the user account can reach. Privileged mode only sets the criteria for asking, but does not limit what a command can reach once approved. One approval qualifies your entire account.

states.label: Sandbox on
states.body: The Bash sandbox is the boundary that the operating system places around shell commands and is turned on with /sandbox. Because boundaries are enforced by the operating system during command execution rather than by inspection of app code, the same restrictions apply to child processes spawned by approved commands. It is based on built-in Seatbelt on macOS and bubblewrap and socat on Linux and WSL2. For the same reason, you can run commands within the sandbox without being asked each time. The default write scopes are the working directory and temporary directory, and protected paths are write-blocked. Read should be shortened to denyRead since most devices are open by default, which also includes the credential file. The network has no direct routes; the proxy only passes accepted domains. Accepted domains are initially empty. The sandbox only wraps shell commands. Built-in tools and hooks such as Read, Edit, and WebFetch, and the local MCP server, which is an external tool server running on my computer, run externally and must be controlled separately with permission rules.

screens.outro: Permission mode determines the criteria for asking, and sandbox determines the reach after execution. Next, we will look at protecting the cloud environment.

screens.title: Cloud environment security and prompt injection response
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, an explanation appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Cloud sessions run in Isolated virtual machine managed by Anthropic. GitHub credentials are not available within the session VM and are limited to the session scope of short term qualification only. The proxy rejects branch deletions and pushes outside of branches, and all operations remain within audit log. Thanks to this protection, any session misconfiguration results in damage confined within the session scope. Network commands such as curl and wget are not automatically approved by default for prompt injection. Scripts handling unfamiliar external services are recommended to run within the VM. However, users remain responsible for reviewing and approving commands and changes prior to execution. The fact that the environment is isolated does not mean that reviews can be omitted.

terms.tip: A separate execution environment for each session. Prevents actions in one session from affecting other sessions or the user's device.
It is a qualification that is only valid for session scope and does not last long. Even if it is leaked, the period and scope of use is narrow.
A record of everything that happened in a session. It serves as a basis for reviewing what happened when an accident occurred.
This is an attack that leads the agent to take unintended actions through instructions hidden in the content the agent reads.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the protection afforded by the environment, let us analyze the rulings when rules overlap.

screens.title: Analysis: When priorities overlap
screens.lead: As you select each question, the decision and reasons will unfold. Decide for yourself first and then unfold it. There is nothing to enter or submit.

items.prompt: If deny Bash (git push *) and allow Bash (git push origin main) are combined, what happens to git push origin main?
items.answer: It is rejected. deny is evaluated first, and if it matches, the result is determined. Just because allow is more specific doesn't take precedence.

items.prompt: What happens when ask Bash (git push *) and allow Bash (git push origin main) come together?
items.answer: Request confirmation. The ask rule requires confirmation first, even if there is a more specific allow. This property serves as a safety device for commands that affect the outside world.

items.prompt: Will deny rules apply in bypassPermissions mode as well?
items.answer: Applies. Even if the mode changes to allow all, the deny rule remains alive. Therefore, regardless of the mode, it is recommended to block commands that must never be executed with a deny rule.

items.prompt: What happens if I call a tool that isn't on the whitelist in dontAsk mode?
items.answer: Rejected without question. Since only pre-allowed tools are executed, it operates predictably in unmanned CI.

items.prompt: Can an allow rule break a protected path write or a critical path delete?
items.answer: It's impenetrable. Protected paths are not automatically approved by allow rules. This default protection ensures that even if you write the rules broadly, the most important paths remain. However, rather than memorizing a list of protection routes, it is more important to first decide which route you want to protect when writing rules.

screens.outro: Now that we've sorted out our priorities, let's apply them to an example.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Without and with a sandbox
screens.lead: Move the slider to see how the damage range changes with different levels of protection in the same situation.

visual.alt: A diagram comparing the damage range without and with a sandbox in concentric circles.

stops.body: The agent approves and executes the installation script of the received repository. This script reads ~/.ssh and attempts to send it to the outside. Without a sandbox, scripts can read and write anywhere the user's account can reach, as well as the network. A single approval will expand the scope of damage to your entire account.

If you run the same script inside a sandbox, writing will be restricted to the working directory and network access will be restricted to accepted domains only. Even if the script tries to send data to the outside world, if it is not an accepted domain, the proxy will block it and the outflow path will be closed.

However, reading is open by default, so the script itself may not be blocked from reading ~/.ssh. You should set denyRead and credential protection together to reduce reads. Turning on the sandbox does not mean that all risks disappear. Knowing what risks remain is the starting point for setup.

The same approval has different meaning depending on whether it is inside or outside the sandbox. Inside the sandbox, the risk of approval is limited to the boundaries, while outside the sandbox it is allowed for the entire account. So both privileged mode and sandbox are needed. In a cloud environment, isolated VMs and session-scoped short-term entitlements play the same role.

screens.outro: Now that we've seen the effectiveness of the sandbox, let's organize which combination to choose for each type of task.

screens.title: Explanatory example: Choosing modes and isolation for each type of task
screens.lead: Select each tab to see combinations of privileged modes and isolation depending on the type of task.

tabs.label: Check unfamiliar code
tabs.body: See all the action directly in Manual mode. Since the goal is to read code, supervision is more important than speed. For steps that require execution, an isolated environment or sandbox is used.

tabs.label: Local iterative development
tabs.body: Overlay sandbox auto-allow on acceptEdits or Manual mode. Editing continues without prompting, and shell commands are executed only within the boundaries of the sandbox, limiting the scope of damage.

tabs.label: CI Automation
tabs.body: Write dontAsk and correct whitelist. Questions shouldn't pop up because there's no one there, and tools that don't allow it should be rejected. The key is to keep your whitelist narrow to only the commands you need.

tabs.label: Isolated environment only mode
tabs.body: Consider bypassPermissions only on isolated containers or VMs. Since this mode does not ask questions, it is only safe if the environment limits the extent of damage. Make sure there are no sensitive credentials in your environment, leave the deny rule alone.

tabs.label: Transition while working
tabs.body: The mode can be changed even within one task. For example, you can navigate in plan mode to make a plan, approve the plan, and implement it by changing it to acceptEdits. This is because different stages require different levels of supervision. You'll be safe as long as you make sure your sandbox settings and deny rules remain the same whenever you switch.

tabs.label: Set on two axes
tabs.body: Mods set a balance between comfort and oversight, while sandboxes and environmental isolation set limits to the extent of damage. Thinking about these two axes separately makes the choice easier. Choosing one of the two and leaving out the other is the most common design mistake. The looser the mode, the tighter the isolation must be, and in environments with weak isolation, the mode must be conservative.

screens.outro: Now that we've outlined the selection criteria, let's gather the highlights.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Select a sentence and check the evidence
screens.lead: If you select each summary sentence, the evidence will unfold. There is nothing to enter or submit. It's a good idea to first say the meaning of the sentence yourself and then unfold it.

items.prompt: Permission rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, and allow, and the one that matches first is applied.
items.answer: Specific rules do not take precedence. Bash (aws *) deny blocks even narrower allows, and ask rules require confirmation first, even if there is a more specific allow. deny also applies to bypassPermissions.

items.prompt: Privileged mode balances convenience and oversight, while sandbox limits the scope of damage.
items.answer: A mode is what you ask for, and a sandbox is what you reach once it's launched. Since they are different axes, one does not replace the other. The two must be decided together. The looser the mode, the tighter the isolation should be; if the isolation is weak, the mode should be more conservative.

items.prompt: Sandboxes restrict file and network access to shell commands and control other tools with rules.
items.answer: Built-in tools and hooks such as Read, Edit, WebFetch, and the local MCP server run outside the sandbox. Neither denyRead nor allowedDomains restrict these tools, so permission rules are required.

items.prompt: bypassPermissions is only used on isolated containers or VMs.
items.answer: This is a permissive mode, so it is only safe if the environment limits the extent of damage. Cloud Sessions complements this with isolated VMs, short-term entitlements, push limits on proxies, and audit logs, but leaves the user responsible for reviewing commands and changes. This responsibility does not diminish whichever mode you use. In summary, rules, modes, and sandbox are three layers of defense with different tasks.

screens.outro: Lastly, let's think about it in relation to our own work.

screens.title: Connect to my work
screens.lead: This screen is for reading only. Read the questions and think for yourself. You will not enter or submit an answer.

paragraphs: Key terms in this lesson are permission rules, permission modes, sandboxes, and file and network isolation. Let's go back to the original question. Where do you draw the line between convenience and oversight, and what enforces that line?

The answer is not one means, but a combination. The determination of each call is determined by the permission rules, the frequency of the request is determined by the permission mode, and the reach after approval is determined by the sandbox and environmental isolation. If any one is missing, that point becomes a weakness. If you write down the three means in a table, you can easily find where you are missing.

Imagine an environment where I use a coding agent. You can check what mode you are using, whether there are any commands blocked with deny, and the folders and domains that shell commands can reach. It's also worth checking to see if the path where your credentials are located is not readable. Also check whether you really need the domains on your whitelist.

When changing settings, start small. After making changes, check whether the rule has been applied as intended using a verification method such as /permissions. Open it narrowly at first, widen it one by one as the need arises, and record the reason for the widening. And remember, no matter what setting you use, you are responsible for reviewing commands and changes before approving them. Rules and sandboxes are intended to reduce mistakes, not replace review.

callout.label: Questions to Think About
callout.text: Where does my work get stuck with permission rules? Think about whether there are any folders that your agent can read that should not be readable, and whether he or she is habitually pressing the approval request button.

checks.q: Pair the following permission modes with the right uses:
right: Conforms to CI by only allowing pre-approved tools and rejecting the rest
Allow all mode used only on isolated containers or VMs
Used for sensitive tasks or when directly reviewing all actions.
Browsing is focused on reading, and editing is blocked before plan approval.
It does not ask for file editing and common commands such as mkdir, mv, and cp.
checks.explain: The mode strikes a balance between convenience and oversight. bypassPermissions allows everything, so consider only isolated environments.
checks.intro: Each permission mode provides a different degree of oversight to the user. Match mode with purpose.
checks.correctFeedback: All are correct. You made a good distinction between the order of decreasing supervision as convenience increases and the isolation conditions for bypassPermissions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatched pair. Note that plan is for navigation with blocked editing, dontAsk is for CI that only allows pre-approved tools, and bypassPermissions is for isolated environments only.

checks.q: Which of the following is correct when turning on the Bash sandbox?
options: All tools, including Read, Edit, and WebFetch, run inside a sandbox.
Read should be reduced to denyRead as most devices are open by default, which also includes the credential file.
The network is open to all domains by default and the proxy blocks only risky domains.
Turning on the sandbox eliminates the need for privileged mode
checks.explain: The sandbox places operating system boundaries only on shell commands. Writes are working directory-centric, but reads are wide open by default and require denyRead.

wrong.0: The sandbox only wraps shell commands, and Read, Edit, WebFetch, etc. are executed outside.
wrong.2: The network proxy only passes through allowed domains, and the whitelist is initially empty.
wrong.3: Permission mode is a separate axis that determines the criteria for asking, and sandbox determines the scope of reach.

checks.intro: See how far the Bash sandbox protects you.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. The sandbox is bounded only to shell commands, and reads are wide open by default and need to be shortened to denyRead.
checks.incorrectFeedback: Sandbox does not wrap all tools, nor does it replace privileged mode. Remember that this applies to shell commands and that the read scope must be narrowed separately.

checks.q: The settings include deny Bash (git push *) and allow Bash (git push origin main) and are running in bypassPermissions mode. What if the agent tries to git push origin main?
options: Since it is in bypassPermissions mode, it is executed by ignoring all rules.
There is a conflict between deny and allow, so the user is asked for confirmation every time.
deny matches first, so it is rejected
checks.explain: Rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, and allow, and the matching result is determined first. There is no priority for being more specific, and the deny rule also applies to bypassPermissions.

wrong.0: Specific rules do not take precedence.
wrong.1: The deny rule also applies to bypassPermissions.
wrong.2: Instead of checking in case of conflict, deny matches first and is rejected. Requesting confirmation is an ask rule.

checks.intro: The deny and allow rules conflict, and bypassPermissions is also turned on. Consider the order of evaluation.
checks.correctFeedback: That's right. Rules are evaluated in the order of deny, ask, and allow, and the deny that matches first is applied, and deny is also valid in bypassPermissions.
checks.incorrectFeedback: It's easy to think that the more specific rules win, but specificity is not the criterion. Note that the evaluation order is deny first and that deny applies regardless of mode.

glossary.def: This is a rule that determines tool calls as Allow, Ask, or Deny. It is evaluated in the order of deny, ask, and allow, and the one that matches first is applied.
It is a standard setting that determines the scope of execution without asking. There are default, acceptEdits, plan, auto, dontAsk, bypassPermissions.
A boundary by which the operating system limits the scope of file and network access for shell commands.
A restriction that limits the scope of writes to the working directory and only allows accepted domains to pass through to the proxy.
Protections that cloud sessions provide, such as isolated VMs, short-term entitlements on session scope, push limits on proxies, and audit logs.

misconceptions.myth: A more specific allow rule beats deny.
misconceptions.fact: deny is evaluated first, so it wins regardless of specificity. A narrow allow cannot bypass a wide deny.
The mode is just a criterion to ask. Sandboxes and environmental containment determine the reach of approved commands.

misconceptions.myth: The sandbox wraps all of the agent's tools.
misconceptions.fact: It only wraps shell commands. File tools, hooks, and the local MCP server (external tool connection server) run externally and must be separately controlled by permission rules.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: Permission rules are evaluated in the following order: deny, ask, then allow, with the matching first being applied.
Privileged Mode balances convenience and oversight, while Sandbox limits the scope of damage.
Sandboxes restrict file and network access to shell commands, and other tools are controlled by rules.
bypassPermissions is only used on isolated containers or VMs.
closing.reflectionLead: This is a question to think about for yourself. It will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where does my work get stuck with permission rules?
